glucocorticoid levels in the blood affect avoidance behavior in rats.
the glucocorticoid hormones have a significant effect on avoidance performance.

glucocorticoids increase the frequency of long interresponse times, decrease the frequency of short interresponse times (and hence increase the mean interresponse time), decrease the variability of interresponse times (i.e. increase the stability of responding), decrease total responses, and increase the number of shocks.

the effects of ACTH and dexamethasome on avoidance behavior.
the effects of ACTH and dexamethasore on free-operant behavior.
the effects of ACTH and dexamethasome on avoidance behavior and on the relationship between glucocorticoids and avoidance behavior in the rat.

glucocorticoids have a direct effect on the avoidance behavior of the rat.
the effects of ACTH or dexamethase are to reduce the frequency of short interresponse times and increase the frequency of long ones.
glucocorticoids exert an inhibitory effect on free-operant performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the avoidance performance was more efficient and stable when glucocorticoid levels were high.

the glucocorticoids have a general inhibitory effect on the frequency of responding and on the variability of the interresponse times, and that the effect of the glucocorticoid on the frequency of short interresponse times depends on the level of glucocorticoid in the blood.
glucocorticoids have a biphasic effect on behavior, with low and high levels of glucocoricoids having opposite effects on behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
glucocorticoids are not just stress hormones.
ACTH and dexamethasome can be used to alter avoidance behavior in rats, and that this behavior is sensitive to glucocorticoid changes.
